newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zurich widens scope with Scudder buy.
newsitem.headline: Zurich widens scope with Scudder buy.

text.p: Zurich Group's deal to acquire U.S. asset manager Scudder, Stevens & Clark will round out the Swiss group's investment management business, analysts said on Friday.

The insurer, Switzerland's largest when total premiums are taken into account including those from outside the country, said it agreed to acquire privately-owned Scudder in a transaction valued at more than $2 billion.
The deal is Zurich's second major purchase of an investment company in less than two years and highlights its determination to be a force in the U.S. investment management sector.

The transaction combines Zurich Group's Chicago-based Zurich Kemper Investments Inc subsidiary, which has some $80 billion in assets under management, with Scudder's $120 billion mutual fund and asset management operation.
Zurich completed its acquisition of Kemper in January 1996.

Zurich's stated strategic direction is toward offering "tailored solutions for financial protection and investment management". It has been actively expanding in both in asset management and in reinsurance.

"(Zurich Group chief executive Rolf) Hueppi has always said that he regarded life insurance as an asset accumulation business and this side of the coin will become more and more important in the future," Pictet & Cie insurance analyst Thomas Della Putta said.
The combination is optimal in that between 70 and 80 percent of Kemper's business is in retail mutual funds while some two-thirds of Scudder's business in institutional, he added.

The acquisition also provides Zurich's Kemper with Sudder's direct distribution capabilities and clients along with greater exposure in the faster growing equity fund and international fund business segments, Della Putta said.
Over 80 percent of Kemper's business is in fixed income and money market funds, a segment not growing very fast, he said.
Analysts raised questions about the fairness of the price and what is being paid beyond the $867 million cash payment.
The deal calls for Zurich to own 69.5 percent of the new company, Zurich Kemper Investments Inc, and for senior employees of Scudder Kemper to hold the remaining 30.5 percent.

"The new firm, headquartered in New York City, will be core to Zurich's global investment management, significantly strengthening Zurich's market position in mutual funds and asset management and strategically positioning the Zurich Group to capitalise on the investment management opportunities emerging throughout the world," Zurich Group said in a statement.

"Strategically this makes sense of course, but the purchase price is not yet clear and we don't yet know about the underlying profitability of Scudder," UBS insurance analyst Thomas Kalbermatten said.
The company plans a news conference at 1200 GMT to discuss the deal. It plans a conference call to analysts at 1400 GMT.
Della Putta said the purchase is a boost for Kemper, which was struggling to build its market share in the United States. But he too was curious about why Scudder decided to sell to Zurich.
He also believed the deal would not be dilutive for Zurich, but if there were a mild dilutive effect, the longer-term benefits would outweigh this setback.
"What is more important is the strategic impact, which is much more important than a possible minor dilution in 1998."
Societe Generale euities and derivatives research said it was leaving its "cautious" EPS estimates for Zurich unchanged at 27.5 francs in 1997, 32.8 in 1998 and 39.9 in 1999.
"Strategically, this operation is positive given that asset management is one of the branches being developed by the group, as is reinsurance," it said in a research note.

It noted that Zurich shares had advanced 16 percent since rumours of the acquisition first surfaced in May, compared with nine percent for the SMI, "which may indicate that the acquisition is already, at least partially, priced in".
Zurich shares were up 15 to 604 around 1145 GMT.
